newsitem.title: UK: British retailers - racing away or stuck at start?.
newsitem.headline: British retailers - racing away or stuck at start?.

text.p: Anecdotal evidence of a surging recovery in British retail spending mounts by the week, but so far official sales data have painted a much more sedate picture.
Analysts expect that circle to be squared soon with all measures pointing to retail sales heading skywards.
"It's inconceivable that all of the survey evidence is incorrect," said John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International.

A flood of recent evidence, most notably from the Confederation of British Industry and British Retail Consortium, has suggested that consumers have dusted off their wallets, blown out the cobwebs and are spending with a vengeance.
But the latest government statistics on offer showed retail sales actually fell 0.6 percent in July, leaving the year-on-year rate of growth at a paltry 2.2 percent.

Economists said July's disappointing sales followed strong figures for June and said the official series still showed the underlying trend was upwards. Nonetheless, the difference in tone compared with the latest surveys was stark.

Shepperd noted new highs in consumer credit, a firming housing market and bullish CBI and BRC surveys. "No-one is saying it's the 1980s again, but it certainly looks a damned sight firmer than two percent year-on-year sales growth."
The CBI distributive trades survey, released on Thursday, polled 15,000 retailers.
"Can they all be wrong?" Shepperd asked.
The CBI's August trades survey, which showed the balance of firms reporting higher sales than a year ago, was the largest since late 1988. Retailers expect further gains in September.
"The gathering momentum in retail trade during August is a welcome indication that consumer confidence is improving," said Alastair Eperon, chairman of the CBI's distributive trades survey panel.
Eperon noted particularly strong growth in goods related to the housing market -- carpet, furniture and household durables.
"People are spending on big-ticket items," he said.

The British Retail Consortium (BRC) conducts its own survey of retailers. That showed retailers saw a like-for-like sales increase of 5.4 percent in the year to July. Official figures pale in comparison, although surveys are compiled very differently to the official sales data.

"It must be emphasised that there is no close month-on-month correlation between the CBI and ONS figures," said Andrew Milligan, economist at General Accident. But he too said CBI evidence showed a similar but much sharper trend than the ONS.
"The strong CBI report...will encourage buoyant forecasts for a sharp rebound in (August) retail sales," he said. Official August retail sales data will be released on September 18.
The CBI survey showed retailers' stocks at their lowest level since January 1992.

"This supports the view that cutbacks in retailers inventories are largely over and that rapid spending growth is likely to feed through to wholesalers and manufacturers," said Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon Brothers.
On the downside, rampant consumer spending could begin to ring alarm bells on inflation.

Thursday's CBI survey showed retailers were passing on higher prices, albeit from a low level. The balance of firms saying prices were higher than last year was the biggest in more than three years, although that has yet to be reflected in official figures.
Eperon said the price rises reflected cost increases going back several months, adding: "Price competition continues to be very strong indeed on the high street."
